title: Trump and Tech Giants Agree to 'Self-Police' AI
paragraphs: US President Donald Trump has announced that the leaders of several major technology companies have signed an agreement to "self-police" the development of artificial intelligence.

The announcement followed a meeting at the White House on September 29, 2026. The voluntary agreement was signed by Trump and executives including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, the founder of the AI company xAI.

Under the agreement, the companies will take several voluntary steps. They will put "robust internal controls" in place and work with independent external auditors to check whether those controls are effective. In addition, each company will set up a committee within its board of directors to review the auditors' reports. The agreement also suggests that, over time, it may make sense to turn these steps into laws and regulations. However, some of the measures were already being carried out by the companies.

Trump described the agreement as "morally binding" and suggested that a committee of about 10 people would be appointed to watch over the whole effort. He also said he was seeing tremendous self-policing.

Earlier the same day, Trump had said that the US government would not limit the development of AI or support "guardrails" or other restrictions, describing AI as a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution.

At the meeting, Amodei said that AI has very real risks, but that the mechanism for addressing those risks was still under discussion. Meanwhile, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in a separate interview that his company was pacing its progress, which sometimes included not training a model. The day before the meeting, OpenAI had stopped the release of a new AI model because of safety concerns.

However, some experts are doubtful. Robin Jia, a computer scientist at the University of Southern California, said he was skeptical about putting so much faith in self-policing. Alex Pascal of Harvard's Berkman Klein Center described the agreement's language as vague and argued that legal responsibility and regulation are needed to reduce the risks of AI. On the other hand, Shri Narayanan, also of USC, said the agreement balances room for innovation with regulation.
